reason: A opens with a single sustained scene aboard the Zong and lets the courtroom, the Barbados code, the Jamaican ledger and Haiti fall out of it as consequences, so the reader is carried by a story that keeps widening. B is an informative survey that cycles through Charleston, ledgers, statutes, the Brookes, Bois Caiman and abolition, restating the same thesis (law converts persons into property) in each new section without narrative momentum. B is also more repetitive at the paragraph level and ends on a stray, garbled sentence about the Code Noir date, while A closes on a genuine argumentative turn.
